Article 49 of the 1995 Constitution of Azerbaijan provides that everyone has the right, having notified the respective governmental bodies in advance, to assemble with other people peacefully and without arms, to organise meetings, demonstrations, protests and marches, and to stage pickets.

Under Article 5 of the Law on Freedom of Assembly of 13 November 1998, advance written notification is required in order to agree on the place and time of an assembly and the route of a march, with the purpose of enabling the relevant local executive authority to take necessary measures.
Under Article 5 of the Law on Freedom of Assembly of 13 November 1998, the notification has to be done in writing five days before the demonstration.

Article 8 §§ IV and V of the Law on Freedom of Assembly of 13 November 1998 provides the relevant local executive authority with broad powers to issue relevant orders so as to prohibit a public assembly.
Article 8 § VI of the Law on Freedom of Assembly of 13 November 1998 provides the relevant local executive authority with broad powers to issue relevant orders so as to stop a public assembly.

Article 9 §§ II and VII of the Law on Freedom of Assembly of 13 November 1998 provides the relevant local executive authority with broad powers to restrict or change the place, route and/or time of a public assembly.
Article 9 § VI of the Law on Freedom of Assembly of 13 November 1998 provides the relevant local executive authority with broad powers to designate specific areas for public assemblies.

At the material time, Article 375.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences provided that a defender and a representative shall be allowed to participate in administrative-offence proceedings from the time an administrative-offence report is drawn up.

At the material time, Article 375.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences provided that if an individual is subjected to an administrative arrest for committing an administrative offence, a defender shall be allowed to participate in the administrative-offence proceedings from the moment of the administrative arrest.

At the material time, Article 376.2 of the Code of Administrative Offences provided that if it is impossible for the lawyer chosen by the person against whom administrative-offence proceedings are being carried out to attend, a judge shall appoint a lawyer for that person in accordance with the legislation of the Republic of Azerbaijan.

At the material time, Article 376.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences provided that if a person subjected to an administrative arrest has no possibility to hire a lawyer due to his or her financial situation, his or her legal assistance shall be funded by the State, and in this case a lawyer may not refuse to carry out his or her duties.

At the material time, Article 396.1 of the Code of Administrative Offences provided that an authorised official may use administrative arrest as a measure to prevent administrative offences, to establish the identity of a person, to draw up an administrative-offence report if this cannot be done at the place of the administrative offence and if the drawing up of a report is important, to ensure the correct and timely examination of administrative-offence cases, and to ensure the implementation of decisions in administrative-offence cases.

At the material time, Article 398.1 of the Code of Administrative Offences provided that administrative arrest, that is the short-term restriction of an individual's liberty, may be applied in exceptional circumstances when deemed necessary for ensuring the correct and timely examination of an administrative-offence case or for the implementation of a decision in an administrative-offence case, except for instances set out in legislation.

At the material time, Article 410.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences provided that an individual who is subject to administrative-offence proceedings or a representative of a legal entity shall be given an opportunity to familiarise himself with the administrative-offence report.

At the material time, Article 410.4 of the Code of Administrative Offences provided that an individual who is subject to the administrative-offence proceedings or a representative of a legal entity has the right to a copy of the administrative-offence report.

At the material time, Article 414.2 of the Code of Administrative Offences provided that a report concerning an administrative offence punishable by administrative detention shall be sent to a judge for examination immediately after it has been drawn up.

At the material time, Article 422.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences provided that cases concerning an administrative offence punishable by administrative detention shall be examined on the day of receipt by the court of an administrative-offence report.

At the material time, Article 422.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences provided that cases against persons subjected to administrative arrest shall be examined at the latest within 48 hours of their arrest.
Under Article 368 of the Code of Administrative Offences, a public prosecutor has the right to participate in administrative proceedings.
Chapter 28 of the Code of Administrative Offences enumerates the participants of administrative proceedings and their rights and obligations.

Chapter 28 of the Code of Administrative Offences does not mention the prosecution — a police officer, public prosecutor or any other public official representing the prosecution — as a participant of the proceedings.

The Commissioner for Human Rights of the Council of Europe continued to receive reports of threats, harassment, and violence against journalists or youth activists in Azerbaijan since the publication of his 2010 report.

One of the Commissioner for Human Rights of the Council of Europe's recommendations to the Azerbaijani authorities was to end practices of unjustified or selective criminal prosecution of journalists or others who may express critical opinions.
The Ganja City Court sentenced youth activist and candidate in the 2010 parliamentary elections Bakhtiyar Hajiyev to two years in prison on 18 May 2011 for evading military service.

According to the Commissioner for Human Rights of the Council of Europe's document CommDH(2011)33 of 29 September 2011, the timing of Bakhtiyar Hajiyev's arrest and the charges against him appear to be indicative of an attempt to stop his activities, which were critical of the Government.

Jabbar Savalan, a member of the youth group of the Azerbaijan Popular Front Party, was sentenced on 4 May 2011 to two and a half years imprisonment by the Sumgait City Court on drug possession charges, after marijuana was said to be found in his possession.
Jabbar Savalan's sentencing occurred soon after he had posted several critical comments against the authorities and called for protests via social networks.
Several international governmental and non-governmental organisations voiced their concerns about what they considered to be fabricated charges against Jabbar Savalan.

According to the Commissioner for Human Rights of the Council of Europe's document CommDH(2011)33 of 29 September 2011, in the past months several national and international NGOs had faced difficulties in carrying out their activities freely in Azerbaijan, and some of them had even been obliged to cease their activities.

A building where several human rights organisations were located, including the Office of the Institute for Peace and Democracy, was demolished on 11 August 2011 in the framework of a reconstruction programme being implemented in Baku.

The building's occupants were unable to retrieve any of their belongings, and their working materials — such as computers, documents, and books — were destroyed during the demolition on 11 August 2011.

According to the Commissioner for Human Rights of the Council of Europe's document CommDH(2011)33 of 29 September 2011, the circumstances of the demolition, which occurred in the evening, give reason to believe that it was carried out in retaliation against the activities of Leyla Yunus, the director of the Institute for Peace and Democracy and owner of the house, who was an outspoken critic of corruption and forced evictions in Azerbaijan.

According to the Commissioner for Human Rights of the Council of Europe's document CommDH(2011)33 of 29 September 2011, the Commissioner's attention was drawn to the wave of arrests of activists and political opponents in connection with protests held in Baku in March and April 2011.

According to the Commissioner for Human Rights of the Council of Europe's document CommDH(2011)33 of 29 September 2011, the protests in Baku in March and April 2011 were sometimes dispersed with excessive force, and the work of journalists was hindered.

According to the Commissioner for Human Rights of the Council of Europe's document CommDH(2011)33 of 29 September 2011, the organisers of protests in Baku in March and April 2011 were denied permission to demonstrate in a central square and other places in the city centre in Baku, and were instead authorised to hold a demonstration in the outskirts of the city.

The Commissioner for Human Rights of the Council of Europe criticised on various occasions the method of curbing the impact of a demonstration by allowing it to take place only at another time and at a less central location, thereby diminishing significantly the visibility of the rally and its message to the general public.

According to the report CommDH(2013)14 of 6 August 2013 by Nils Muižnieks, Commissioner for Human Rights of the Council of Europe, in recent years the Azerbaijani authorities have arrested and prosecuted online media actors, notably bloggers or social media activists, in moves which have often been described as retaliation against their online activities.

According to the report CommDH(2013)14 of 6 August 2013, bloggers Adnan Hajizadeh and Emin Milli were arrested in early September 2009 for hooliganism after having posted a video on YouTube which was critical of the government.

According to the report CommDH(2013)14 of 6 August 2013, the issue of limitations imposed on freedom of assembly has regularly been raised by local and international observers in recent years, with the most frequent problems including the banning of demonstrations in central and easily accessible locations and the use of force to disperse demonstrations, leading to arrests and in some cases harsh sentences.

According to the report CommDH(2013)14 of 6 August 2013, the Azerbaijani authorities confirmed that the legislation does not require permission for rallies, but the authorities appear to have interpreted it as requiring such permission, and a system of authorisation has in practice replaced the system of notification.

According to the report CommDH(2013)14 of 6 August 2013, peaceful protesters have been effectively banned from demonstrating in central Baku since 2006, despite advanced notification of the assemblies.

According to the report CommDH(2013)14 of 6 August 2013, several requests by the political opposition or civil society to hold demonstrations were allegedly denied or, when allowed, organisers were obliged to have them in areas very remote from the city centre.

Resolution 1917 (2013) of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe, adopted on 23 January 2013, noted that there is no political dialogue with the opposition parties outside parliament in Azerbaijan.

Resolution 1917 (2013) of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe expressed concern about the restrictive climate for the activities of the extra-parliamentary opposition in Azerbaijan, which complains about limitations imposed on freedom of expression and freedom of assembly and the lack of access to the public media.

Resolution 1917 (2013) of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe stated that the establishment of an inclusive political system and a truly competitive and unrestrictive political environment requires full implementation of basic freedoms, including freedom of expression, freedom of assembly and freedom of association.
Resolution 1917 (2013) of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe expressed deep concern about the situation regarding basic freedoms in Azerbaijan.

Resolution 1917 (2013) of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe expressed alarm at reports from human rights defenders and domestic and international non-governmental organisations about the alleged use of fabricated charges against activists and journalists in Azerbaijan.

Resolution 1917 (2013) of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe stated that the combination of the restrictive implementation of freedoms with unfair trials and the undue influence of the executive results in the systemic detention of people who may be considered prisoners of conscience in Azerbaijan.

The European Parliament Resolution of 12 May 2011 on Azerbaijan (P7_TA(2011)0243) noted that a wide-ranging clampdown on freedom of expression and assembly was being carried out in Azerbaijan following the peaceful protests against the government on 11 March and 2 April 2011.

The European Parliament Resolution of 12 May 2011 on Azerbaijan noted that the clampdown included arrests, harassment and intimidation of civil society activists, media professionals and opposition politicians in Azerbaijan.
The European Parliament Resolution of 12 May 2011 on Azerbaijan noted that the cases of activists Jabbar Savalan and Bakhtiyar Hajiev were of particular concern.

The European Parliament Resolution of 12 May 2011 on Azerbaijan expressed deep concern at the increasing number of incidents of harassment, attacks and violence against civil society and social network activists and journalists in Azerbaijan.

The European Parliament Resolution of 12 May 2011 on Azerbaijan strongly deplored the practice of intimidating, arresting, prosecuting and convicting independent journalists and political activists on various criminal charges in Azerbaijan.
The European Parliament Resolution of 12 May 2011 on Azerbaijan deplored the arrest of around 200 people prior to, and during, the anti-government protests of 2 April 2011 in Baku.
The European Parliament Resolution of 12 May 2011 on Azerbaijan called on the Azerbaijani authorities to allow peaceful protest as well as freedom of assembly.
The European Parliament Resolution of 12 May 2011 on Azerbaijan deplored the physical violence used against protesters at the anti-government protests of 2 April 2011 in Baku.

The European Parliament Resolution of 12 May 2011 on Azerbaijan called on the Azerbaijani authorities to maintain a dialogue with members of civil-society organisations and to allow individuals to freely engage in peaceful, democratic activities.

The European Parliament Resolution of 12 May 2011 on Azerbaijan encouraged the Azerbaijani authorities to allow peaceful demonstrations to take place in relevant locations and urged them to refrain from intimidating the organisers by detaining them and charging them with criminal and other offences.

The European Parliament Resolution of 12 May 2011 on Azerbaijan regretted that some youth activists had been expelled from Baku State University after missing examinations while in police custody linked to their political activities.

According to the Amnesty International public statement EUR55/003/2011 of 31 March 2011, ahead of the 2 April protest organised by opposition political parties through Facebook, the Azerbaijani authorities detained at least 11 prominent political activists on 31 March 2011.

According to the Amnesty International public statement EUR55/003/2011 of 31 March 2011, the wave of arrests began on 29 March when Nazim Abbasli from the Azerbaijan Democrat Party was arrested and given five days' administrative detention.

According to the Amnesty International public statement EUR55/003/2011 of 31 March 2011, Elchin Salimov, a member of the youth wing of opposition party Musavat, was arrested on 31 March 2011 by police and questioned about the 2 April rally, and was sentenced to seven days' administrative detention.

According to the Amnesty International public statement EUR55/003/2011 of 31 March 2011, Rauf Mammadov, a member of the youth wing of opposition party Musavat, was arrested on 31 March 2011 by police and questioned about the 2 April rally.
According to the Amnesty International public statement EUR55/003/2011 of 31 March 2011, police questioned the family of Musavat member Idris Emiraslanli in an attempt to ascertain his whereabouts.

According to the Amnesty International public statement EUR55/003/2011 of 31 March 2011, Deputy Chairman of the Azerbaijan Popular Front Party Ilham Huseynli was arrested on 31 March 2011 and remained in custody that evening.

According to the Amnesty International public statement EUR55/003/2011 of 31 March 2011, Azerbaijan Popular Front Party members Karim Mehdiyev, Mehdi Mehdiyev and Nemat Aliyev were arrested on 31 March 2011 and remained in custody that evening.

According to the Amnesty International public statement EUR55/003/2011 of 31 March 2011, Classical Popular Front Party member Yagub Babanli and youth activists Khalid Amanli, Rovshan Nasili, and Tabriz Qasimov were all arrested on 31 March 2011 and remained in custody that evening.

According to the Amnesty International public statement EUR55/003/2011 of 31 March 2011, Ilham Huseynli, Nemat Aliyev, Tabriz Qasimov and Mehdi Mehdiyev were given sentences ranging between five and seven days' administrative detention, convicted of resisting police or disturbing the public order despite the fact that the protests had yet to take place.

According to the Amnesty International public statement EUR55/003/2011 of 31 March 2011, Amnesty International was concerned that the trials of those arrested on 31 March 2011 were held behind closed doors.

According to the Amnesty International public statement EUR55/003/2011 of 31 March 2011, several youth activists who posted the announcement of the protest on the internet were arrested on questionable charges and convicted in trials that reportedly failed to meet international standards in connection with the March 11 protest.

According to the Amnesty International public statement EUR55/003/2011 of 31 March 2011, the call for protests on 2 April 2011 met with a new wave of violence and intimidation directed against activists and journalists.

According to the Human Rights Watch news release of 1 April 2011, Azerbaijani authorities detained at least 10 opposition activists in an effort to prevent a public rally planned for 2 April 2011 in Baku.
According to the Human Rights Watch news release of 1 April 2011, police detained the activists on 31 March 2011 in Baku and various provinces.
According to the Human Rights Watch news release of 1 April 2011, the protests planned for 2 April 2011 were organised by Azerbaijan's opposition parties and young social network users.

According to the Human Rights Watch news release of 1 April 2011, the activists were quickly convicted in summary trials on charges of disobeying police orders and sentenced to administrative detention ranging from five to thirteen days, which would keep them locked up beyond the protest date.

According to the Human Rights Watch news release of 1 April 2011, police in Sumgait rounded up at least two activists: Ibrahim Mammedzade, a political activist who ran in the November 2010 parliamentary elections, and Elchin Salimov, an opposition Musavat party youth activist.
According to the Human Rights Watch news release of 1 April 2011, police went to Ibrahim Mammedzade's home on the morning of 31 March 2011 but did not find him there.

According to the Human Rights Watch news release of 1 April 2011, Ibrahim Mammedzade later went to the Sumgait Municipal Police Department on his own accord, together with his lawyer, Asabali Mustafayev.

According to the Human Rights Watch news release of 1 April 2011, after about an hour-long conversation with the deputy police chief, in which Ibrahim Mammedzade was asked about his educational background and political activities, the deputy police chief assured lawyer Asabali Mustafayev that Mammedzade would not be detained.

According to the Human Rights Watch news release of 1 April 2011, later in the day police detained Ibrahim Mammedzade, and a court sentenced him to seven days' administrative detention for allegedly disobeying a police order.
According to the Human Rights Watch news release of 1 April 2011, the trial of Ibrahim Mammedzade was closed, and the judge refused to wait for lawyer Asabali Mustafayev to arrive.

According to the Human Rights Watch news release of 1 April 2011, lawyer Asabali Mustafayev told Human Rights Watch that Elchin Salimov had been picked up at home in the early hours of 31 March 2011 and sentenced to seven days of administrative detention for disobeying a police order.

According to the Human Rights Watch news release of 1 April 2011, the Mobile Group of Lawyers reported that other activists detained in Baku on 31 March 2011 and convicted of disobeying police orders included: Rovshan Nasirli, blogger and active social network user, sentenced by the Yasamal District Court to nine days; Namat Aliyev, opposition Popular Front Party member, sentenced to seven days by the Nizami District Court; Khalid Amanli, an opposition Musavat party youth activist, sentenced to eight days by the Yasamal District Court; and Kerim Mehdiyev, the driver for the opposition Popular Front Party leader, sentenced to 13 days by the Binagadi District Court.

According to the Amnesty International press release of 2 April 2011, according to local rights groups six more activists had been detained on 1 April 2011 in connection with the protest, bringing the total number of those arrested before the protest to 17.

According to the Amnesty International press release of 2 April 2011, Vugar Hasanli, Teymur Abbasli, Ibrahim Ahmadzade and Tahir Abdullayev were arrested by police late on 1 April 2011, picked up by officers from their homes in and around Baku.
According to the Amnesty International press release of 2 April 2011, Vugar Hasanli was sentenced to 10 days' administrative detention.
According to the Amnesty International press release of 2 April 2011, Ibrahim Ahmadzade was sentenced to 7 days' administrative detention.

According to the Amnesty International press release of 2 April 2011, at least seven individuals were sentenced to administrative detention, most under Article 310.1 of Azerbaijan's Code of Administrative Offences which bans wilful disobedience of a police official.
According to the Amnesty International press release of 2 April 2011, the majority of the trials took place behind closed doors, without the defendants having access to legal representation.

According to the Amnesty International press release of 2 April 2011, John Dalhuisen stated that the fact that key organisers were being arrested in advance and sentenced in closed trials of offences that had yet to take place was indicative of the length to which the authorities were prepared to go to silence dissenting voices.

According to the Amnesty International press release of 2 April 2011, political activists Arzu Musayev and Kifayet Musayev said police had told them not to leave their home district of Gadabay to attend the rally in Baku, and that when they did they were followed by police officers all day.
According to the Amnesty International press release of 2 April 2011, Azerbaijan state TV reported that the 2 April protest was an attempt by foreign powers to destabilise Azerbaijan.
According to the Amnesty International press release of 2 April 2011, state controlled television stations broadcast several programmes depicting Facebook users as mentally ill.

According to the Amnesty International report EUR55/011/2011 of 2011, the Azerbaijani authorities brought questionable criminal charges against Vidadi Isgandarov, a human rights defender, and opposition leader Shahin Hasanli, with the timing of their arrests and the dubious nature of the charges strongly suggesting they were targeted for their political activities and the peaceful exercise of their rights to freedom of expression and assembly.

According to the Amnesty International report EUR55/011/2011 of 2011, Shahin Hasanli, managing board member of the Popular Front Party, was one of those arrested on 31 March 2011 prior to the 2 April opposition rally.
According to the Amnesty International report EUR55/011/2011 of 2011, Shahin Hasanli was convicted on 22 July 2011 and sentenced to two years' imprisonment for the possession of illegal arms.

According to the Amnesty International report EUR55/011/2011 of 2011, Shahin Hasanli, who was one of the main organisers behind the March and April 2011 protests, claimed that the bullets were planted on him by the police at the time of his arrest and maintained that he had been targeted because of his political activities.

According to the Amnesty International report EUR55/011/2011 of 2011, the timing of Shahin Hasanli's arrest a few days before the April 2011 protests, the nature of the charges and the paucity of supporting evidence all point strongly to the conclusion that his arrest was politically motivated.

According to the Human Rights Watch news release of 12 March 2011, in at least three cases the Azerbaijani authorities held activists on administrative charges just long enough to prevent them from participating in the planned protests.

According to the Human Rights Watch news release of 12 March 2011, on 8 March 2011 police detained Rashadat Akhundov, a 27-year-old social media activist who was one of the first to call for the 11 March protest.

According to the Human Rights Watch news release of 12 March 2011, lawyer Elchin Namazov told Human Rights Watch that police in civilian clothes approached Rashadat Akhundov as he was running errands in Baku and demanded his documents, then grabbed him, twisted his arms, stuffed him into a car and drove away.

According to the Human Rights Watch news release of 12 March 2011, the Khatai District Court convicted Rashadat Akhundov of disobeying police orders and sentenced him to five days of administrative detention.

According to the Human Rights Watch news release of 12 March 2011, on 8 March 2011 police arrested Sahavat Sultanov, deputy head of the opposition party Musavat's youth wing and an active social media user, who had actively promoted the 12 March opposition rally through his Facebook contacts and other outreach.

According to the Human Rights Watch news release of 12 March 2011, police charged Sahavat Sultanov with auto hooliganism — violating traffic rules — and in a hearing that lasted only minutes a judge sentenced him to five days of administrative detention.

According to the Human Rights Watch news release of 12 March 2011, on 4 March 2011 police detained Dayanat Babayev, a member of the opposition Popular Front Party's Youth Committee and an active Facebook and social network user who was critical of the government but promoted peaceful public protests.

According to the Human Rights Watch news release of 12 March 2011, Dayanat Babayev's family and friends heard nothing until 6 March 2011, when they learned that he had been convicted, allegedly for disobeying a police order, and sentenced to 10 days in detention.

According to the Human Rights Watch news release of 12 March 2011, the court ruling stated that Dayanat Babayev had disobeyed police orders and insulted policemen who approached him to warn him not to use foul language while talking on the phone in public.

According to the Human Rights Watch news release of 12 March 2011, lawyer Asabali Mustafayev, who visited Dayanat Babayev in the detention centre on 7 March 2011, said that Babayev was rounded up in an internet café in downtown Baku, where fifteen minutes after he arrived, three plainclothes policemen came in, twisted his arms and took him away with no explanation.

According to the Annual Freedom of Expression Report by the Institute for Reporters' Freedom and Safety of 2012, freelance journalist Fuad Huseynov was arrested in October 2010 on charges of hooliganism after exposing illegal activities of public officials in the Ujar region, in particular involvement in drug trafficking and trafficking in persons.

According to the Annual Freedom of Expression Report by the Institute for Reporters' Freedom and Safety of 2012, on 26 September 2011 Fuad Huseynov was sentenced to six and a half years in prison under Article 221.3 of the Criminal Code.

According to the Annual Freedom of Expression Report by the Institute for Reporters' Freedom and Safety of 2012, one of the victims who testified against Fuad Huseynov later stated that he had been pressured into giving false testimony by a local mafia group.

According to the Annual Freedom of Expression Report by the Institute for Reporters' Freedom and Safety of 2012, Fuad Huseynov had previously served two years of a three and a half year prison sentence on hooliganism charges after he accused a former Ujar city police chief of drug-related crimes.

According to the Annual Freedom of Expression Report by the Institute for Reporters' Freedom and Safety of 2012, blogger and human rights defender Taleh Khasmammadov was arrested on 12 November 2011 in the Ujar region and charged with hooliganism under Criminal Code Articles 221.2.2 and 221.3, as well as resisting arrest under Article 315.1.

According to the Annual Freedom of Expression Report by the Institute for Reporters' Freedom and Safety of 2012, Taleh Khasmammadov was sentenced on 20 April 2012 to four years in prison and is thought to have been targeted for exposing the criminal activities of local officials, including by posting a series of videos to YouTube containing interviews with victims of human rights abuses.

According to the Contact online news release of 31 March 2011, the chief of the press service department of the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Azerbaijan, Orkhan Mansurzade, informed the Turan news agency that attempts to breach public order and to hold a protest on 2 April 2011 at the central streets and squares of Baku without agreement of the Baku City Executive Authority would be vigorously prevented.

According to the Contact online news release of 31 March 2011, the mayor's office refused to give permission to the Ictimai Palata to hold a demonstration on 2 April 2011 in front of Narimanov cinema and proposed to hold the protest in Bibiheybet settlement.
According to the Contact online news release of 31 March 2011, the Ictimai Palata decided to hold the protest at 2 p.m. on 2 April 2011 at the Fountains Square.

According to the Contact online news release of 31 March 2011, in connection with the Ictimai Palata's decision to hold the protest at the Fountains Square on 2 April 2011, arrests of potential activists began.

The Commissioner for Human Rights of the Council of Europe continued to receive reports of threats, harassment, and violence against journalists or youth activists in Azerbaijan since the publication of his 2010 report.

One of the Commissioner for Human Rights of the Council of Europe's recommendations to the Azerbaijani authorities was to end practices of unjustified or selective criminal prosecution of journalists or others who may express critical opinions.
The Ganja City Court sentenced youth activist and candidate in the 2010 parliamentary elections Bakhtiyar Hajiyev to two years in prison on 18 May 2011 for evading military service.

According to the Commissioner for Human Rights of the Council of Europe's document CommDH(2011)33 of 29 September 2011, the timing of Bakhtiyar Hajiyev's arrest and the charges against him appear to be indicative of an attempt to stop his activities, which were critical of the Government.

Jabbar Savalan, a member of the youth group of the Azerbaijan Popular Front Party, was sentenced on 4 May 2011 to two and a half years imprisonment by the Sumgait City Court on drug possession charges, after marijuana was said to be found in his possession.
Jabbar Savalan's sentencing occurred soon after he had posted several critical comments against the authorities and called for protests via social networks.
Several international governmental and non-governmental organisations voiced their concerns about what they considered to be fabricated charges against Jabbar Savalan.

According to the Amnesty International press release of 2 April 2011, Vugar Hasanli, Teymur Abbasli, Ibrahim Ahmadzade and Tahir Abdullayev were arrested by police late on 1 April 2011, picked up by officers from their homes in and around Baku.
According to the Amnesty International press release of 2 April 2011, Vugar Hasanli was sentenced to 10 days' administrative detention.
According to the Amnesty International press release of 2 April 2011, Ibrahim Ahmadzade was sentenced to 7 days' administrative detention.

According to the Amnesty International press release of 2 April 2011, at least seven individuals were sentenced to administrative detention, most under Article 310.1 of Azerbaijan's Code of Administrative Offences which bans wilful disobedience of a police official.
According to the Amnesty International press release of 2 April 2011, the majority of the trials took place behind closed doors, without the defendants having access to legal representation.

According to the Amnesty International press release of 2 April 2011, John Dalhuisen stated that the fact that key organisers were being arrested in advance and sentenced in closed trials of offences that had yet to take place was indicative of the length to which the authorities were prepared to go to silence dissenting voices.

According to the Amnesty International press release of 2 April 2011, political activists Arzu Musayev and Kifayet Musayev said police had told them not to leave their home district of Gadabay to attend the rally in Baku, and that when they did they were followed by police officers all day.
According to the Amnesty International press release of 2 April 2011, Azerbaijan state TV reported that the 2 April protest was an attempt by foreign powers to destabilise Azerbaijan.
According to the Amnesty International press release of 2 April 2011, state controlled television stations broadcast several programmes depicting Facebook users as mentally ill.

According to the Amnesty International report EUR55/011/2011 of 2011, the Azerbaijani authorities brought questionable criminal charges against Vidadi Isgandarov, a human rights defender, and opposition leader Shahin Hasanli, with the timing of their arrests and the dubious nature of the charges strongly suggesting they were targeted for their political activities and the peaceful exercise of their rights to freedom of expression and assembly.

According to the Amnesty International report EUR55/011/2011 of 2011, Shahin Hasanli, managing board member of the Popular Front Party, was one of those arrested on 31 March 2011 prior to the 2 April opposition rally.
According to the Amnesty International report EUR55/011/2011 of 2011, Shahin Hasanli was convicted on 22 July 2011 and sentenced to two years' imprisonment for the possession of illegal arms.

According to the Amnesty International report EUR55/011/2011 of 2011, Shahin Hasanli, who was one of the main organisers behind the March and April 2011 protests, claimed that the bullets were planted on him by the police at the time of his arrest and maintained that he had been targeted because of his political activities.

According to the Amnesty International report EUR55/011/2011 of 2011, the timing of Shahin Hasanli's arrest a few days before the April 2011 protests, the nature of the charges and the paucity of supporting evidence all point strongly to the conclusion that his arrest was politically motivated.

According to the Human Rights Watch news release of 12 March 2011, in at least three cases the Azerbaijani authorities held activists on administrative charges just long enough to prevent them from participating in the planned protests.

According to the Human Rights Watch news release of 12 March 2011, on 8 March 2011 police detained Rashadat Akhundov, a 27-year-old social media activist who was one of the first to call for the 11 March protest.

According to the Human Rights Watch news release of 12 March 2011, lawyer Elchin Namazov told Human Rights Watch that police in civilian clothes approached Rashadat Akhundov as he was running errands in Baku and demanded his documents, then grabbed him, twisted his arms, stuffed him into a car and drove away.

According to the Human Rights Watch news release of 12 March 2011, the Khatai District Court convicted Rashadat Akhundov of disobeying police orders and sentenced him to five days of administrative detention.

According to the Human Rights Watch news release of 12 March 2011, on 8 March 2011 police arrested Sahavat Sultanov, deputy head of the opposition party Musavat's youth wing and an active social media user, who had actively promoted the 12 March opposition rally through his Facebook contacts and other outreach.

According to the Human Rights Watch news release of 12 March 2011, police charged Sahavat Sultanov with auto hooliganism — violating traffic rules — and in a hearing that lasted only minutes a judge sentenced him to five days of administrative detention.

According to the Human Rights Watch news release of 12 March 2011, on 4 March 2011 police detained Dayanat Babayev, a member of the opposition Popular Front Party's Youth Committee and an active Facebook and social network user who was critical of the government but promoted peaceful public protests.

According to the Human Rights Watch news release of 12 March 2011, Dayanat Babayev's family and friends heard nothing until 6 March 2011, when they learned that he had been convicted, allegedly for disobeying a police order, and sentenced to 10 days in detention.

According to the Human Rights Watch news release of 12 March 2011, the court ruling stated that Dayanat Babayev had disobeyed police orders and insulted policemen who approached him to warn him not to use foul language while talking on the phone in public.

According to the Human Rights Watch news release of 12 March 2011, lawyer Asabali Mustafayev, who visited Dayanat Babayev in the detention centre on 7 March 2011, said that Babayev was rounded up in an internet café in downtown Baku, where fifteen minutes after he arrived, three plainclothes policemen came in, twisted his arms and took him away with no explanation.

According to the Annual Freedom of Expression Report by the Institute for Reporters' Freedom and Safety of 2012, freelance journalist Fuad Huseynov was arrested in October 2010 on charges of hooliganism after exposing illegal activities of public officials in the Ujar region, in particular involvement in drug trafficking and trafficking in persons.

According to the Annual Freedom of Expression Report by the Institute for Reporters' Freedom and Safety of 2012, on 26 September 2011 Fuad Huseynov was sentenced to six and a half years in prison under Article 221.3 of the Criminal Code.

According to the Annual Freedom of Expression Report by the Institute for Reporters' Freedom and Safety of 2012, one of the victims who testified against Fuad Huseynov later stated that he had been pressured into giving false testimony by a local mafia group.

According to the Annual Freedom of Expression Report by the Institute for Reporters' Freedom and Safety of 2012, Fuad Huseynov had previously served two years of a three and a half year prison sentence on hooliganism charges after he accused a former Ujar city police chief of drug-related crimes.

According to the Annual Freedom of Expression Report by the Institute for Reporters' Freedom and Safety of 2012, blogger and human rights defender Taleh Khasmammadov was arrested on 12 November 2011 in the Ujar region and charged with hooliganism under Criminal Code Articles 221.2.2 and 221.3, as well as resisting arrest under Article 315.1.

According to the Annual Freedom of Expression Report by the Institute for Reporters' Freedom and Safety of 2012, Taleh Khasmammadov was sentenced on 20 April 2012 to four years in prison and is thought to have been targeted for exposing the criminal activities of local officials, including by posting a series of videos to YouTube containing interviews with victims of human rights abuses.

According to the Contact online news release of 31 March 2011, the chief of the press service department of the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Azerbaijan, Orkhan Mansurzade, informed the Turan news agency that attempts to breach public order and to hold a protest on 2 April 2011 at the central streets and squares of Baku without agreement of the Baku City Executive Authority would be vigorously prevented.

According to the Contact online news release of 31 March 2011, the mayor's office refused to give permission to the Ictimai Palata to hold a demonstration on 2 April 2011 in front of Narimanov cinema and proposed to hold the protest in Bibiheybet settlement.
According to the Contact online news release of 31 March 2011, the Ictimai Palata decided to hold the protest at 2 p.m. on 2 April 2011 at the Fountains Square.

According to the Contact online news release of 31 March 2011, in connection with the Ictimai Palata's decision to hold the protest at the Fountains Square on 2 April 2011, arrests of potential activists began.
